chapter_theme: The second quarter of Pattinathar's antadhi on Ekambar. The love poems of the millet field close with the harvest and the parting (879 to 881), and the poem turns to the devotee's claims: wealth is for the small, kingship without the ash does not shine, a Brahmin without devotion is a hunter and a hunter with devotion is best of all. The centre is a long description of the Lord's half-woman form from feet to crown, right side Siva and left side Uma (888 to 898), followed by the dance, Tillai and Kalatti, and the begging Lord whose bull and skull frighten the women he came to beg from.
structure_note: 879 to 881 end the kurinji sequence of chapter 50 (the trysting place, the lovers as one life, the harvested field). 882 to 887 are claims about devotion against wealth, kingship, Brahmin birth and low birth, with the Ravana story and the eight forms. 888 to 898 describe the Ardhanari form limb by limb, right side the Lord and left side the Lady: feet and body (888), head (890), hair (891), eyes (892), ears (893), shoulders (894), belly and waist (895), garments (896), feet (897), hands (898). 899 and 900 are the dance and its shrines; 901 the Lord's uniqueness; 902 and 903 open the bhikshatana scenes that continue into chapter 52. The speakers of the love verses are supplied from convention.

879.reading: A speaker tells the one of sweet speech to look at the jewel chamber where the lovers embrace, among the shining flower groves, the dancing quail and the waterfall pool on the Kailasa of Ekambar who shot the moving cities, and says the mind is bewildered without ceasing by the haunt the golden one went to and marked out for us.
879.nuance: மணியறை (the jewel chamber) and சூழல் வகுத்து (marking out a haunt) point to the appointed trysting place of the kovai; whether the hero or the girl is bewildered, and who 'went in gold', I can't fix. The verse is a scene more than a statement.

880.reading: The friend says that those who arrange this marriage, like these, will heighten the joy of the wedding day, and asks who could split two who are one dear life, while the one with the honey mouth stands softening with flowers on the Kailasa of Kambar whose waterfall scatters gems, in this surrounded field.
880.nuance: ஆருயிர் ஒன்றாம் இருவரை விள்ள, to split two who are a single life, is the verse's claim about the lovers, and the question who could do it is rhetorical: the match is already made. The marriage arrangers (வகுப்பார்) mark the move from secret love to the open.

881.reading: The friend or girl says that, trusting the field would not wilt, they plucked the soft millet, and now that the heavy-earringed girl's dancing is to end and parting comes, helplessness falls on us and the eyes that melt the mind arrive; the devotees who sing many melodies worship Ekambar in this Kailasa without faltering.
881.nuance: The harvested millet ends the girl's duty of guarding the field and so ends the meetings (புனம் விடுத்தல்); கையறவு, helplessness, is the fixed word for that moment. The last line's singing devotees are the shrine frame, placed against the silence of the lovers.

882.reading: The wealth that reaches small men who are not great of heart belongs only to the small-minded with great deceit; it is not the refuge of the devotees of Ekambar, whose locks hold the Ganga's flood and who fixed the fiery arrow against the forts of the sky.
882.nuance: The verse does not say wealth is evil; it says it goes to the small and the devotees do not lean on it (சார்வு அன்றே). தள்ளம்பு எரி கொண்டு அமைத்தார், who set the fiery arrow, is the Tripura myth used as the Lord's title.

883.reading: Though horses that beat down enemies, rut-streaming hill-like elephants, infantry and chariots gather and shine under the shade of the royal parasol, if the good ash of Kambar is not on their brow, kingship and the royal drum will never shine on the wide earth.
883.nuance: The fourfold army and the parasol are the Kural's apparatus of kingship, and the verse makes them nothing without the ash. The claim is about the ash as the mark of Siva's devotee on the king, not about the ash as a charm; the Tirumanthiram calls the same ash armour.

884.reading: Even if born first among the gods on earth, never parting for a moment from the Veda and its limbs, and tending the sacred fire, those who lack the goodness of joining and worshipping at Ekambam in Kachi, of the Lord who shares his body with Uma of the mountain king's line, stand in the midst of the hunters.
884.nuance: நிலத்து இமையோர், gods on earth, is the honorific for Brahmins, and the verse grants them Veda, limbs and fire before placing them among the வேட்டுவர். It is paired with 885: birth and rite are made to count for nothing in both directions.

885.reading: Though born at the bottom of a clan that kills living things with weapons and eats them, that walks like cattle, without understanding and with little shame, laughing, those who love the anklets of the Lord who owns us at Ekambam in Kachi are the best of all.
885.nuance: The description of the clan is harsh and unqualified, and the verse still ranks its devotee உத்தமர், best for all (யாவர்க்கும்), above the Brahmin of 884. The ground is love for the Lord's feet alone, not conduct, learning or reformed habits.

886.reading: The Lord with the tall elephant's hide made the ten heads and twenty arms of the demon slacken under his toe, and when the demon sang to him with hand and voice, Kachi Ekambar rejoiced and gave him the good sword of the Kailasa people.
886.nuance: The Ravana story is clear in outline; the middle lines, with கையான, கைவாள் and a variant கயிலைகைவாளொடு நாள், are not. The point is the Lord's turn from crushing to gift when the crusher sings, grace following song.

887.reading: Space, wind, fire, water, earth, moon, sun and the atom: the one who has these as his form, who wears the elephant's hide, the Supreme who dwells at Ekambam in Kachi without departing, is the fragrant companion of those devotees of the Supreme who know.
887.nuance: The list is the eight forms (அட்டமூர்த்தம்) of Siva; அணு, the eighth, is taken by tradition as the sacrificer or the soul, and the verse leaves it as 'the atom'. The companion is for அறிவார், those who know, not for all devotees.

888.reading: The twin lotus feet, thighs like coral columns, broad shoulders and chest, the blue in the throat, matted locks like lightning across the cosmos, three holy eyes and a woman embraced on one side: these are the beauties of our Lord Ekambar.
888.nuance: This verse gives the whole form once; 890 to 898 then take it part by part, each time right side the Lord and left side the Lady. பெண் ஒர் பக்கத்து அணைத்தார் announces the Ardhanari form that organizes the series.

889.reading: Those who do not hold to the great who have long matured in knowledge, who know nothing of what is told them of the young Lord's beauty and the victory of Ekambar our father, are struck down by the god of ignorance and lie wasted in the world.
889.nuance: அறியாமை தெய்வம் கிழகு எறியப்பட்டு, 'struck ... by the god ignorance', is the striking phrase; கிழகு is obscure. The verse makes attaching to the wise (பழகு அறிவில் பெரியோர்) the condition of knowing the Lord, not scripture or rite.

890.reading: On one side lies the hissing serpent, on one side the moon; the Ganga with tossing waves is held bound and shines; the konrai and the garland of skulls; the fierce war fought with the sword: such is the crown of matted locks of Ekambar on the bull.
890.nuance: The head carries the standing emblems, serpent, moon, river, konrai, skulls, in a single list; தலைமாலை, the skull garland, keeps the cremation ground in the ornament.

891.reading: Tufted coral locks with the fragrant konrai garland on the right, the crescent of a moon not yet full, Ekambar with thick hair; on the other side gold and gem shoots and the kazhuneer flower woven in: so the beauty of the crest shines.
891.nuance: The right half is the Lord's matted hair and konrai, the left the Lady's dressed hair with kazhuneer and gold; முற்றுற்றிலர் மதியின் கொழுந்து is the crescent as 'the moon that has not reached fullness'.

892.reading: On the right the gracious lotus eye and above it on the brow the flaming eye that shines unsplit, of wealthy Kambar; on the left the dark flower eye of blue, and the musk dot on the brow of the goddess rising to her flower-decked hair.
892.nuance: The third eye is counted on the Lord's half only; the Lady's half has the brow-dot (நுதற் பொட்டு) in its place. அணங்கு names Uma with the word the love verses use for the hill girl.

893.reading: Over the spread hood of the five-headed serpent, a gem earring set with red-rayed stones sways on the right ear; on the left, a long diamond, gems laughing in the sunlight and a red-gold makara earring: these are Ekambar's ears.
893.nuance: The makara earring is the woman's ornament and the serpent-hood with the kundalam the ascetic's; the verse sets them on the two ears of one head.

894.reading: The right shoulder rises like a coral hill that love shakes, the chest shines with ash like a snow-white golden mountain; on the left a soft shoulder joined by pollen-filled hair, scented with fine sandal, and a breast at which a child might murmur: this is Ekambar's beauty.
894.nuance: காது அலைக்கும் (that shakes the ear) and காதல் அலைக்கும் (that love shakes) are both possible for the first words; குதலைக்கும் முலை may be the breast at which a child babbles, or a breast with a soft murmur. The ash on the chest is the one Saiva emblem in the series.

895.reading: The holy belly on the right, firm and strong, of Kambar who with beauty destroyed the three cities of those above and wore down the world that praises him; on the left the ornamented breasts that the body cannot hold, and the young vanji waist that sags: this too is right.
895.nuance: The first line (தரம் பொற்பு அழியும் உலகு அட்டி எய்த்து) is hard; it seems to praise the Lord's strength through the world's exhaustion. நேர் உடைத்தே, 'has rightness', closes the belly-and-waist pair by calling the uneven halves fitting.

896.reading: Over the tiger-skin garment a strong belt is tightened and a loincloth on a cord of munji grass shows: that is the right waist; on the other waist a kanchi girdle is fastened over a royal fine thin cloth: so for the lord who dwells at Ekambam with the strong shining bull.
896.nuance: The ascetic's garb (புலியாடை, கோவணம், முஞ்சி) on the right and the queen's silk and girdle on the left; the Lord's half is dressed as a renouncer, which the Siddhar poets in this corpus take as the garb to be seen through.

897.reading: The right foot is like a red lotus with roaring anklets, set on the neck of thunder-voiced Death; the left foot is like a young shoot and wears anklets softer than cotton: such is the form of the Lord of Kachi Ekambam.
897.nuance: The foot on Death's neck is the Markandeya story, told in full at 908; here it is a mark of the right foot only, while the left is the Lady's. The series that began with the feet (888) returns to them.

898.reading: Shooting down the three cities of the strong and arrogant, pressing Brahma's head, speeding the axe-blade so that ... : the holy bangled hand of Ekambar our father, put on with the holy rope of his serpents.
898.nuance: நெற்களென்றும் பருக்கவற்றாங் in lines 2 and 3 does not resolve for me; the hand's deeds (the bow, the pressing of Brahma, the axe) are clear and the serpent bangle (கடகம்) is the ornament. The Lady's hand is missing from this verse, unless it is in the corrupt lines.

899.reading: With the drum's sound in his hand thundering so that the cosmos above splits, his blood-red foot stamping so that the earth is crushed, his locks spread beyond the directions and the cities, Kambar who grants boons dances the great dance even into the evening.
899.nuance: The dance here breaks the egg and crushes the earth, the destroying dance, and is still வரத்தைத் தரு, boon-giving. எல்லியும் (even at evening) may name the evening dance (சாயரட்சை) of the temple.

900.reading: The three thousand good Brahmins came together and bowed, saying the Lord delighted in the dance and took us to save us, full of love and knowing nothing but their duty; Tillai's hall and Kalatti are his places, but what is sweet to our Lord is Kachi Ekambam where he dwells.
900.nuance: The three thousand of Tillai (Chidambaram) are praised here for love and duty, where 884 set Brahmin birth and rite at nothing; the difference is that these are devotees of the dancer. The verse ranks Kachi above Tillai and Kalahasti, as a shrine poem does.

901.reading: Say that they are sweet, that there are none like them and no others equal: the solitary one who takes form with his lady, the sage who ordained dharma, the three-eyed one who always rejoiced, sweet to Thandi's love, with the hot axe-blade: Kachi Ekambar.
901.nuance: தண்டி is most likely Thandiyadigal, the blind devotee of Arur whose love the Lord rewarded; it could be another Dandi. The verse's claim is uniqueness (ஒப்பார் பிறர் என்ன ஒண்ணாத் தனியவர்) joined to the pair with the Lady, one who is two.

902.reading: Thinking of Kachi Ekambar in praise, the infatuation he works arrives in full; the speaker tells of a cruel one, the son of the first ones, who whips the horse so that the night does not dawn, and of taking even the serpent to set the young women dancing in the courtyard.
902.nuance: The verse does not come together for me: முன்னவர் மகனார் (the son of the first ones) with a horse, a night that does not dawn (விடியா இரவு), the serpent and dancing girls may be the bhikshatana procession or a Kama figure. The one plain claim is the first line, that the Lord himself makes the மையல்.

903.reading: Seeing the bull that leaps with a crack and the laughing skull on your head, the young women take fright and scatter, you of Ekambam; and before the five-mouthed hooded serpent that hisses they fear still more: how then, beggar, will any alms come to you?
903.nuance: The begging Lord (பிட்சாடனர்) is addressed by the women he begs from, the Thirumurai convention in which they mock what frightens them. The question is teasing: the emblems that make him the Lord are what keep the alms away. The scene continues in 904 and 905.

links.note: The Kural's king with all six, army, people, wealth, ministers, allies and fort, stands among kings as the male leads its herd; Pattinathar grants the same horses, elephants, infantry, chariots and parasol and says kingship and drum never shine without Kambar's ash on the brow. One condition is added that the Kural does not have.

Both make the ash the real protection: Tirumular calls it armour (கவசம்) that ends deeds and brings the Siva state; Pattinathar makes it the one thing without which an army and a parasol cannot make a king shine. Tirumular's gain is release, Pattinathar's is the kingdom's lustre.

Both rank the Brahmin of Veda and the six duties below the devotee: Tirumular says feeding ten million such Brahmins does not equal a handful given to the ash-wearing servant; Pattinathar says the Brahmin who keeps the Veda and the fire but does not worship at Ekambam stands among the hunters.

Both deny that birth sets rank: the Kural says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from what one does; Pattinathar says one born at the bottom of a killing, flesh-eating clan is best of all if he loves the Lord's anklets. The Kural's measure is work, Pattinathar's is devotion, and both set it against descent.

Both make devotion override every other mark: Tirumular's ash-wearers who cry 'our master' are gods walking on earth; Pattinathar's lowest-born lover of the Lord's anklets is உத்தமர் for all. Pattinathar goes further by naming the clan's killing and shamelessness and still ranking its devotee first.

The same Ravana story in the same two beats: Arunagirinathar's Ravana pulls up Kailasa, has his twenty arms crushed under one toe and is afterwards given a sword by Siva; Pattinathar's demon has ten heads and twenty arms slackened under the toe and, when he sings, receives the good sword.

Both make the dance a destruction: Tirumular's dance in the golden hall is the dissolution of the world; Pattinathar's drum splits the cosmos and his foot crushes the earth. Tirumular adds that the dance is bliss and wonder; Pattinathar that it grants boons.

The three thousand Brahmins of Tillai (Puliyur) appear in both as the Lord's worshippers: Arunagirinathar's three thousand worship daily by sacrifice; Pattinathar's bow together and know nothing but their duty. Pattinathar praises them for love where 884 set Brahmin rite at nothing.

source_issues: 886 has a variant note கயிலைகைவாளொடு நாள் for line 3, and the printed line is hard to construe.
899 line 3 reads போர்ப்பச்ச்சடை with a doubled ச், apparently போர்ப்பச் சடை.
The love verses 879 to 881 and the bhikshatana verses 902 and 903 have no speaker marked.
